prime.problem: Starting with Attention Is All You Need leaves Q, K and V floating: the paper assumes you already know what a token is, where its vector comes from, what the model outputs and how one output becomes the next input. Without that route in your head, every later paper is a box with no arrows going in or out.
prime.fits: It's the spine of the hub's model cards. Each stop links to a card that teaches it in depth (z2h tokenizer, embeddings, attention, sampling), and it is the first item of Day 1.5 on the inference path.
expect: embedding rows and why similar tokens end up close
the autoregressive loop and its KV cache
prime.goal: Trace any prompt from text to generated text and give the shape of the data at every stop, then say which paper explains each stop.

attend: Why does the table give 7 for the token count of our prompt rather than 29 or 6, and what decides where the cuts fall?
The embedding table is used twice in this model. Where is the second time, and what does it turn the last vector into?
If attention on its own can't tell first from last, where does Qwen put the order back in, given that it has no position table?
Which steps of the answer were uncertain, and why is Delhi at 0.994 once New has been chosen?
On the The capital of India is step, why does top-p 0.9 keep 5 tokens while top-k 2 keeps 2, and which tokens does that let through?

must: Text is cut by learned merges (BPE) → each piece is an integer ID → the ID selects one row of the embedding table → the model only ever works with those vectors, never with letters, which is why spelling and digits behave oddly

Attention mixes tokens together but ignores order → order has to be injected (learned positions, sinusoids, RoPE rotating Q and K, or ALiBi's distance bias) → without it, India of capital would look the same as capital of India

One block = attention (tokens read earlier tokens) + feed-forward (each token on its own), both added back through a residual → the block repeats 24 times with the shape fixed at tokens × 896 → only the last position's vector is turned into 151,936 logits

Logits → softmax → a decoder picks one token → it's appended and the model runs again → each new token is P(tₙ | t₁…tₙ₋₁) → earlier tokens' K and V are cached, so each new step adds about 12 KB of memory instead of recomputing the prefix
elevated: The embedding table is also the output layer (tied weights) → it holds 136M of the 494M parameters → in a small model, vocabulary size is a big share of the size, and that share shrinks as the model gets wider and deeper
Sampling from the full distribution keeps the long tail → here 0.09 of the probability sat below the top-p 0.9 cut → over many steps, pure sampling lands in the tail often, which is why top-p exists
reference: Qwen2.5-0.5B: 24 layers, hidden 896, 14 query heads, 2 KV heads, head dim 64, FFN 4,864 (SwiGLU), vocab 151,936 (151,665 used)
the paper per stop: BPE (Sennrich 2015), SentencePiece, word2vec, RoFormer, ALiBi, Attention Is All You Need, MQA, GQA, FlashAttention 1–2, Switch Transformers, GPT-3, Holtzman et al. 2019

compress.prompt: Closed book, draw the route as one line of arrows from text to generated text, and write the data's shape under each arrow for our 7-token prompt. Then add one sentence on where order enters and one on what makes it a loop.
checklist: order is added inside attention by RoPE, not by a separate table
attention + feed-forward, repeated 24 times; the shape stays 7 × 896
last vector → 151,936 logits → softmax → a decoder picks one token
the token is appended and the model runs again until end-of-text
earlier tokens' K and V are cached rather than recomputed

retrieve.q: Explain why reading Attention Is All You Need first is harder than following one prompt through the model first.
answer: the paper assumes tokens, embeddings, softmax and decoding
it describes a 2017 encoder-decoder translation model, not today's decoder-only LLMs
following one prompt gives each stop an input and an output you can check, so Q, K and V attach to something concrete

retrieve.q: Walk the token India from the moment the text is typed until it influences the next-token logits. Name each stop and what it does to the data.
answer: the tokenizer emits the piece India (leading space included) with ID 6747
row 6747 of the 151,936 × 896 table becomes its vector
in each of 24 blocks, later tokens' queries read its key and value (with RoPE encoding its position), and the feed-forward rewrites its vector
its information reaches the last position through attention; only the last vector is projected to logits

retrieve.q: On the step after The capital of India is, choose a decoder for (a) a factual Q&A API and (b) brainstorming city names. Justify each with the card's numbers.
answer: (a) greedy or low temperature: New is 0.698, and T = 0.7 lifts it to 0.869; beam 4 gave the same answer
(b) top-p around 0.9 with T ≥ 1: keeps 5 tokens, so variety stays but the 0.09 tail is cut
pure sampling (no cut) produced off-topic continuations on 4 of 4 seeds

retrieve.q: The base model gave its first answer token only 0.277. Why so low, and would a chat model behave differently?
answer: a base model only continues text: after a question it may answer, repeat or ask another question ( The, India, What)
a chat model is fine-tuned on a template where an answer follows the question, so its first token is far more certain
the pipeline is identical; only the weights differ

compare.q: That card cuts a code-token distribution at p = 0.95 and keeps 5 tokens. Here p = 0.9 also keeps 5. What does that say about how top-p sizes its set, and what would top-k 5 do on each?
answer: top-p sets the size by cumulative mass, so the count depends on how peaked the distribution is
here two tokens hold 0.862 and three small ones close the gap; there the mass was spread more evenly
top-k 5 keeps 5 in both cases whatever the shape, including tokens the model barely believes in

compare.q: nanoGPT adds a learned position vector to each token vector. Qwen has no position table. What does each one do, and what does RoPE gain?
answer: nanoGPT: wte[id] + wpe[pos], added once at the input, limited to the trained length
Qwen: rotates Q and K in every attention layer by an angle set by the position
after the rotation the dot product depends on the distance between tokens, which carries over to longer contexts better

predict.q: Make the prompt twice as long, 14 tokens instead of 7. Which of these change: the hidden shape between blocks, the number of logits used to pick the next token, the model's parameter count, the KV cache before the first answer token? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: The hidden shape becomes 14 × 896, and the KV cache doubles from 7 × 12 KB = 84 KB to 168 KB. The parameter count stays at 494M: weights don't depend on prompt length. The number of logits used stays at 151,936: the model scores every position, but only the last row picks the next token. That is why prompt length costs memory and prefill time but not model size.

apply.task: Using only the card's step-9 probabilities ( New 0.698, Delhi 0.164, known 0.018, Mumbai 0.015, not 0.013): (1) apply top-k 3 and give the rescaled probabilities; (2) apply top-p 0.8 and say how many tokens survive; (3) compute the KV cache per token for Llama-3.1-8B (32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dim 128, bf16), the same way the card does for Qwen.
apply.done: Top-k 3 gives 0.793 / 0.186 / 0.020 (dividing by 0.880). Top-p 0.8 keeps 2 tokens, because 0.698 + 0.164 = 0.862 ≥ 0.8, so the rescaled values are 0.81 and 0.19. Llama-3.1-8B: 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 × 2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KB per token, about 10.7× Qwen's 12 KB.
apply.hint: KV bytes per token = layers × KV heads × head dim × 2 (K and V) × 2 bytes. Query heads don't appear, which is the whole point of GQA.
